content.statement: A GET request should not change data on the server.

remember: GET is a safe method: crawlers, prefetchers and retries send it freely, so changes belong in POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.

content.prompt: POST /api/users has just created a new user. Which status code fits the response best?

options.text: 200 OK
202 Accepted
201 Created
204 No Content

remember: 201 Created says a new resource now exists; its URL goes in the Location header.

content.prompt: Match each status code with its meaning.

right.text: The target resource does not exist
An unexpected failure on the server
Success, with no body to return
A new resource was made

remember: 2xx means success, 4xx means the client's request is at fault, 5xx means the server failed.

content.prompt: Three of these need a changed request to succeed. Which one may succeed if the same request is retried later?

remember: 503 is a temporary server problem worth retrying later; a 400, 413 or 415 fails again until the request changes.

content.prompt: A client sends PUT /docs/7 with If-Match: "v3", but another user has already saved version "v4". What should the server answer?

options.text: 409 Conflict
412 Precondition Failed
428 Precondition Required
304 Not Modified

remember: When an If-Match condition fails, the server skips the change and answers 412; that is how HTTP prevents lost updates.

content.statement: In a REST API, GET, PUT and DELETE can all be sent to the same URL, such as /orders/7.

remember: One URL names one resource; the method says whether to read, replace or delete it.

content.prompt: What do the query parameters in GET /api/orders?status=open&sort=-created do?

options.text: Filter and sort the list of orders
Create a new order with status open
Update every order that is still open
Select a different version of the API

remember: Query parameters narrow, sort and page a collection; they never turn a GET into a change.

content.prompt: Three of these URLs follow REST naming. Which one does not?

remember: REST URLs are nouns for resources; the verb belongs in the HTTP method, not in the path.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the client learns the URL of the order it just created.
content.code:
POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"productId": 5, "quantity": 2}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
____: /api/orders/981

options.text: Referer
Origin
Host
Location

remember: A 201 response names the new resource's URL in the Location header.

content.prompt: Match each request with what it does in a REST API.

right.text: Change only the fields sent in the body
Remove order 7
Create a new order
Replace order 7 with the body

remember: POST creates in a collection, PUT replaces the whole resource, PATCH changes part of it, DELETE removes it.

content.statement: If the frontend form already validates the input, the API can trust the data it receives.

remember: Anyone can call the API directly with curl or a script, so the server validates every input itself.

content.prompt: POST /api/users receives {"email": "not-an-email"}. What should the API do?

options.text: Save the user and let them fix the email later
Answer 400 and name the invalid field
Answer 500, because the data is broken
Drop the email and save the rest

remember: Bad input is the client's mistake: reject it with 400 and say which field is wrong, before doing any work.

content.prompt: What does this print?

options.text: ['name is required']
['name is required', 'age must be 18+']
['age must be 18+']

remember: Collect every field error and return them together, so the client can fix them all in one go.

content.prompt: A customer ordered a quantity of -5 and was credited money instead of charged. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Convert quantity with parseInt before the check
Validate productId before loading the product
Also reject quantity < 1 in the condition

remember: Check both ends of a numeric range; a check for 'too large' alone lets zero and negative values through.

content.prompt: A sort column cannot be passed as a query parameter, so it goes into the SQL text. Fill the blank so the endpoint is safe from SQL injection.

options.text: sort.length > 20
typeof sort !== "string"
!SORTABLE.includes(sort)
sort.includes(";")

remember: Values that cannot be bound as parameters, like a sort column, must match an allow-list of known values.

content.statement: A 500 response should include the exception's stack trace so client developers can debug faster.

remember: Log the stack trace on the server and send the client only a generic message plus an id it can quote.

content.prompt: Why should every endpoint return errors in the same body shape, such as Problem Details?

options.text: Errors in one shape are smaller and faster to send
Browsers reject error bodies in any other format
It lets the server skip setting a status code
Clients can handle every error with one piece of code

remember: One error shape across all endpoints means one error handler on every client.

content.prompt: While the database was down, the dashboard of 5xx responses stayed at zero and the app, which checks response.ok, showed "Saved". Find the bug.

fixes.text: Send the error with res.status(500).json(...)
Log the error after sending the response
Send err.message instead of "save failed"

remember: A failure needs a failing status code; a 200 with an error in the body looks like success to clients and monitoring.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
class AppError(Exception): pass
class NotFound(AppError): pass
class Conflict(AppError): pass

STATUS = [
    (AppError, 500),
    (NotFound, 404),
    (Conflict, 409),
]

def status_for(err):
    for cls, status in STATUS:
        if isinstance(err, cls):
            return status
    return 500

print(status_for(NotFound()), status_for(KeyError()))

remember: Check the most specific error types first; a base class checked first matches every subclass.

content.prompt: Sign-up fails: the e-mail is already taken. Which of these belongs only in the server log, not in the response?

items.text: A trace id the user can quote to support
The name of the unique index the INSERT violated
The field that caused the error: email

remember: Translate internal failures such as a violated index into client terms like 'e-mail already taken'; schema details stay in the log.

content.statement: A 401 Unauthorized response means the user is signed in but may not perform this action.

remember: 401 means the server does not know who you are; 403 means it knows and still says no.

content.prompt: Which of these checks is authorization rather than authentication?

options.text: Comparing the password with the stored hash
Verifying the signature of a JWT
Looking up the session id from the cookie
Checking that the user owns the invoice they asked for

remember: Authentication answers who is calling; authorization answers whether that caller may do this particular thing.

content.prompt: Order the steps of a password login that uses a server-side session.

steps.text: The server stores a new session with a random id
The browser sends the cookie with every later request
The client sends the e-mail and password over HTTPS
The server compares the password with the stored hash
The server returns the session id in an HttpOnly cookie

remember: Verify the password, create the session, hand back only its id in an HttpOnly cookie, and look it up on every request.

content.prompt: Match each item with its role in authentication.

right.text: Short-lived credential sent with every API call
Stops page JavaScript from reading the cookie
Stored instead of the password itself
Longer-lived secret used only to get new access tokens

remember: Store hashes, not passwords; keep access tokens short-lived and renew them with a separate refresh token.

content.prompt: Any signed-in customer can read other customers' invoices by changing the id in the URL. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Return 403 instead of 404 when no invoice is found
Add AND customer_id = $2 and pass req.user.id
Switch invoice ids from numbers to random UUIDs

remember: Being signed in is not permission: scope every lookup to what the caller owns, or anyone can walk the ids.

content.statement: Middleware runs in the order it was registered, so its position in the pipeline matters.

remember: Middleware runs in registration order; anything a handler depends on must be registered before it.

content.prompt: In an Express-style app, the authentication middleware is registered after the route handlers. What happens to a request for a protected route?

options.text: The handler answers without checking who is calling
The framework moves authentication to the front
Every request is rejected with 401
The request hangs until it times out

remember: Middleware only guards what comes after it; register authentication before the routes it protects.

content.prompt: What does this print?

options.text: A1 A2 B1 B2 handler
A1 B1 handler A2 B2
A1 B1 handler B2 A2
A1 B1 B2 A2 handler

remember: Middleware wraps the rest of the pipeline: code after await next() runs on the way back out, in reverse order.

content.prompt: Every request, even GET /api/health, hangs until the client times out. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Register express.json() before this middleware
Mark the middleware function as async
Call next() after setting req.startedAt

remember: A middleware must either send a response or call next(); doing neither leaves the request hanging.

content.prompt: A browser app on another origin calls this API with a bearer token. Order the middleware from first to run to last.

steps.text: Authorization: checks the user's role
Route handler
CORS: answers preflight OPTIONS requests
Authentication: validates the token, sets the user

remember: CORS goes before authentication, because the browser's preflight request carries no token and would get 401.

content.statement: Sending DELETE /api/orders/7 twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once.

remember: DELETE is idempotent: the second call may answer 404, but the state is the same as after the first.

content.prompt: Which of these requests is not idempotent?

options.text: PUT /carts/3/items/9 with {"qty": 2}
PATCH /accounts/9 with {"balance": 50}
PATCH /accounts/9 with {"add": 10}
DELETE /carts/3/items/9

remember: Idempotency depends on what a request does: setting a value is safe to repeat, adding to it is not.

content.prompt: An app sends POST /payments and the connection drops before the response arrives. How can it retry without risking a double charge?

options.text: Retry with the same Idempotency-Key header; the server replays the stored result
Retry as PUT /payments, because PUT is idempotent
Wait 30 seconds so the first request can finish, then retry
Send a fresh random id with each retry so the server can tell them apart

remember: An idempotency key lets the server recognise a retry and replay its stored response instead of doing the work again.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Check-then-act with an await in between lets concurrent duplicates through; claim the key atomically before doing the work.

content.prompt: Order what the server does with a POST /payments request that carries an Idempotency-Key.

steps.text: Charge the card
Look up the key; if a finished response is stored, return it
Send the response to the client
No stored response: claim the key by inserting it as in progress
Save the status code and body under the key

remember: Claim the key before the work and save the response before sending it, so every retry finds the claim or the stored result.

content.statement: When a client asks for limit=1000000, the API should return that many rows.

remember: The server enforces a maximum page size; a client cannot use a huge limit to download the whole table at once.

content.prompt: GET /api/products could return two million rows. What is the usual fix?

options.text: Return one page at a time, with a limit and a way to get the next page
Compress the response so the two million rows download faster
Raise the server timeout so the query has time to finish
Keep the full two-million-row response cached in memory

remember: Large lists are returned in pages of bounded size, with a way to ask for the next one.

content.prompt: Page 1 is fetched, a new row is inserted, then page 2 is fetched. What does this print?

remember: With offset pagination, a row inserted before the current position pushes the others down, so the next page repeats a row.

content.prompt: Posts are listed newest first. :last_id is the id of the last post on the previous page. Fill the blank to get the next page.
content.code:
SELECT id, title
FROM posts
WHERE id ____ :last_id
ORDER BY id DESC
LIMIT 20;

remember: A cursor continues from the last row seen in the sort direction: with ORDER BY id DESC the next page has smaller ids.

content.prompt: A bulk import gave thousands of orders the same created_at. Some of those orders never appear on any page. Find the bug.
content.code:
def next_page(db, cursor):
    # cursor: created_at of the last order shown
    return db.fetch_all(
        """
        SELECT id, created_at, total
        FROM orders
        WHERE created_at < %(cursor)s
        ORDER BY created_at DESC
        LIMIT 50
        """,
        {"cursor": cursor},
    )

fixes.text: Use <= instead of < in the WHERE clause
Raise the LIMIT so all tied rows fit on one page
Sort and compare on (created_at, id) and keep both in the cursor

remember: A cursor needs a unique sort key; add the id as a tie-breaker, or rows that share a timestamp get skipped.

content.statement: A rate limiter that rejects a request should answer with 500 Internal Server Error.

remember: Over the limit is answered with 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with Retry-After saying when to come back.

content.prompt: What is the main reason to rate-limit a login endpoint?

options.text: To slow down attackers who guess passwords
To make each successful login faster
To remove the need for hashing passwords
To make sure no login request ever fails

remember: Limiting attempts per client or account makes brute-force password guessing too slow to work.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the client knows how many seconds to wait.
content.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/problem+json
____: 30

{"title": "Too many requests"}

options.text: Expires
Cache-Control
Keep-Alive
Retry-After

remember: Retry-After on a 429 tells the client how long to wait, in seconds or as a date.

content.prompt: The limit is 3 requests per minute. What does this print?

remember: A fixed window resets at its boundary, so a client can send twice the limit within seconds around the edge.

content.prompt: Match each rate-limiting algorithm with its behaviour.

right.text: Refills at a steady rate and allows bursts up to its capacity
Lets queued requests out at a constant rate, smoothing bursts
Stores a timestamp per request: exact, but memory grows with traffic
One counter per period: cheap, but bursty at the period edge

remember: Fixed windows are cheap but bursty at the edge, sliding logs are exact but costly, buckets trade burst size against a steady rate.

content.statement: A cached value updates itself automatically when the database row it came from changes.

remember: A cache does not watch your database; a value stays stale until its TTL runs out or your code deletes it on write.

content.prompt: Building the leaderboard takes 2 seconds and every request asks for it. What does a server-side cache add?

options.text: It keeps the built leaderboard so later requests reuse it until it expires
It makes the database run the 2-second query faster
It stores a copy of the leaderboard in each player's browser
It builds every possible leaderboard when the server starts

remember: A cache stores a computed result so repeated requests skip the expensive work until the value expires.

content.prompt: Order the steps of a cache-aside read when the value is not cached yet.

steps.text: Store the value in the cache with a TTL
Look the key up in the cache and miss
Return the value to the caller
Build the cache key from the request
Load the value from the database

remember: Cache-aside: check the cache, on a miss load from the database, store the result with a TTL, then return it.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Until its TTL runs out, a cached value hides changes in the database; pick the TTL by how stale the data may be.

content.prompt: Under load, a renamed user sometimes shows the old name for up to an hour. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Lower the TTL in getUser to 60 seconds
Delete the cache entry after the database update
Run the delete and the update together with Promise.all

remember: Delete the cached value after the write; deleting first lets a concurrent read cache the old row again for a full TTL.

content.statement: Moving slow work such as sending e-mail to a background queue lets the API respond without waiting for it.

remember: Put slow side work on a queue and answer the request right away; a worker does the rest.

content.prompt: Your queue delivers every job at least once, so a job may run twice. What must the job handler be?

options.text: Idempotent, so a second run changes nothing
Fast enough to finish within the request timeout
Running on the same server as the API
Wrapped in a try/catch that hides every error

remember: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen; write jobs so running them twice does no extra harm.

content.prompt: Three of these tasks are good candidates for a background job. Which one should stay in the request?

items.text: Resizing an uploaded photo into thumbnails

remember: Work the response depends on stays in the request; work the user can wait for goes to a queue.

content.prompt: If reserving stock fails, the order is rolled back, but the customer still gets a receipt e-mail. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Enqueue the job after tx.commit() succeeds
Delay the job by 5 seconds so the transaction can finish
Wrap queue.add in its own try/catch

remember: Enqueue a job only after the transaction commits, or use an outbox; otherwise workers act on data that was rolled back.

content.prompt: Order the steps of the transactional outbox pattern for sending an order e-mail.

steps.text: A relay reads the outbox row and puts the job on the queue
Commit the transaction
Begin a database transaction
A worker takes the job and sends the e-mail
Insert the order and an outbox row in the same transaction

remember: With an outbox, the job is saved in the same transaction as the data, so it exists exactly when the data does.

content.statement: When changing one module regularly forces changes in several others, those modules are tightly coupled.

remember: Modules that keep changing together are coupled; loosen them so each can change on its own.

content.prompt: In a layered backend (API, Application, Domain, Infrastructure), which dependency breaks the rule that dependencies point inward?

options.text: An endpoint calls a use case from the application layer
The Order domain class imports the Postgres client to save itself
Infrastructure implements an interface the application layer defines
A use case creates and changes Order objects from the domain

remember: The domain depends on nothing; databases and frameworks sit at the edge and depend inward on it.

content.prompt: Match each coupling smell with the change that loosens it.

left.text: A service reads another module's tables directly
Business rules live inside HTTP handlers
A class creates its own database client with new
Endpoints return database entities as they are

right.text: Pass the client in through the constructor
Map entities to response DTOs
Call that module's public API instead
Move the rules into a use case the handler calls

remember: Use other modules' public APIs, inject dependencies, keep rules out of handlers and map entities to DTOs.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the orders module needs no change when another module starts reacting to new orders.

options.text: await bus.request("billing.charge", order)
await bus.publish("send-receipt", { to: order.email })
await bus.publish("order.placed", { id: order.id })
await billing.charge(order); await email.send(order)

remember: Publishing a fact like order.placed lets new consumers subscribe without touching the publisher; a command names its receiver.

content.prompt: Three of these tightly couple services A and B. Which one does not?

items.text: B reads A's tables in A's database
A calls B over HTTP and fails while B is down
A and B share a library of database entities
B consumes A's versioned events and keeps its own copy

remember: Shared databases, shared entity libraries and synchronous call chains couple services; versioned events with local copies keep them apart.
